newsitem.title: KENYA: Burundi ousted president says to work for peace.
newsitem.headline: Burundi ousted president says to work for peace.

text.p: Burundi's ousted president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, who left the U.S. embassy on Sunday after taking refuge there for 11 months, condemned the coup that ousted him from power and said he wanted all-party talks.

Ntibantunganya, speaking on Thursday night in his first interview since the coup last July, said he would continue to struggle for democracy and was prepared to work for peace with all sides including military leader Pierre Buyoya.

"I will work for peace, security and the development of my people. I put my intelligence, my force, my energy at the service of the people in Burundi," Ntibantunganya told Reuters by telephone from Bujumbura.

"The things that I stood for before I still stand for. I believe in democracy and in a free political life. I want our society to be improved. We need mutual respect. There should be no exclusion. This is my vision," he said.
Ntibantunganya, an ethnic Hutu, fled to the U.S. embassy fearing he would be killed two days before a coup by the Tutsi-dominated army last July 25 forced him from office and installed Buyoya.

African leaders, who imposed sanctions against Burundi shortly after the coup, effectively recognised Buyoya as president at an Organisation of African Unity summit in Zimbabwe this month. Sanctions were relaxed in April.

Ntibantunganya emerged from the embassy on Sunday in a complex deal with Buyoya by which he received security guarantees, a house overlooking Lake Tanganyika, cars and bodyguards and the promise of a return to political life.
"I am happy to leave the embassy, but I will be happier if my departure accelerates the search of the different parties for peace," he said.
Burundi's state-owned media ignored Ntibantunganya's exit from the embassy and local authorities have cancelled his first news conference scheduled for Friday, aides said.

Ntibantunganya's party Frodebu, which won elections in June 1993 on the back of Burundi's Hutu majority, has been sidelined since the coup as Buyoya in April announced a pre-ceasefire agreement with the main armed Hutu group, the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
"I am against the coup, but I invite him (Buyoya) now to respect the law, to negotiate, because it is the only way forward to resolve the problems of Burundi," Ntibantunganya said.
Asked if Buyoya was a partner he said: "Absolutely. I also consider CNDD as a partner and everyone else. They are all partners for me."

"One must support the negotiation process. But negotiations must be global...That means they must engage all parties and not be limited just to armed groups. All the parties in the conflict must be there from the beginning," he said.
More than 150,000 people -- mainly civilians -- have died in Burundi since October 1993 when Tutsi troops murdered the country's first elected Hutu president in an attempted coup.
Ntibantunganya was chosen president in 1994 when Burundi's next Hutu president was killed along with Rwanda's leader when their plane was shot down, sparking the Rwandan genocide.
Aides to the ousted leader continue to call him "president", but Ntibantunganya refused to claim the title directly, arguing the question should be decided through negotiation.
"Never, never, never should Burundi be ruled by force. That cannot be so, but the most important thing is to negotiate and to respect the law. Above all I respect the law," he said.
"We were in the process of creating a tradition of reconciliation and a coup d'etat reversed that conciliation process," he said.
In a sideswipe at Buyoya he said the revolution in the former Zaire had been indispensable because no people should be subjected to tyranny.
